methods.text: Stop each session mid-step so the next one starts easily.
Keep a log of every decision with its reason, one line each.
Make the cheapest version that could fail, and watch how it fails.
Fix one known defect before adding anything new.
Read the work aloud and change every line you stumble on.
Trace every number on the page back to its source before showing it.
Set the deadline at half the time, then use the rest only for fixes.
Describe the finished work in writing first, then compare it at the end.

constraints.text: Every result shows the date and time it was calculated.
Every field states the range of values it accepts.

tasks.text: Churn cost calculator: customers, monthly loss rate, and average value per customer give the revenue lost each year and what a one-point cut in the rate would save.
Rework cost calculator: cases per month, error rate, and cost to fix each error give the monthly cost of mistakes and the saving if the rate fell by half.
Price rise tester: current price, volume, and margin give how much volume the buyer could lose after a price rise and still earn the same profit.
Tool overlap finder: the buyer's software tools with cost and main job give a list of overlaps and the yearly spend on duplicate tools.
Handoff counter: each step of a process with who does it gives the number of handoffs between people and the waiting time those handoffs add.
Cash gap estimator: monthly costs, billing terms, and typical payment delays give the cash the buyer needs to cover the gap between paying out and getting paid.

temperaments.text: Repeats the other side's point before answering it.
Asks what it costs before asking if it works.
Keeps steering back to the original question.
Splits every question into smaller ones.

guests: historical | Euclid | State a few assumptions, then build everything from them. | died c. 270 BC
historical | Ibn al-Haytham | Trust nothing until an experiment shows it. | died c. 1040
temperaments: Agrees fast, then quietly does it their own way.
Argues the opposite side to test an idea.
methods: Design the error and empty states first.
List the assumptions in the brief and check each one.
Make it work in black and white before adding color.
Take the conventions of a genre and break exactly one.
Write the copy before the layout.
Scope the work to what fits in one day.
constraints: Under 100 words of fixed text on the page.
tasks: Cost-of-inaction calculator: the buyer's current volumes and rates give what the problem costs per month and per year, with each step of the sum shown.
Readiness scorecard: twelve yes-or-no questions give a score out of 100, the three weakest areas, and one next step for each.
Benchmark checker: the buyer's own figures sit next to typical ranges they can edit, with each gap marked ahead, level, or behind.
Leak finder: a funnel of stages with counts gives the stage that loses the most and what fixing half of that loss would be worth.
Time-back calculator: weekly hours on manual tasks and an hourly cost give the hours and money an automated step would return.
Before-and-after map: today's process as a list of steps becomes a side-by-side view marking the steps that could be removed or automated.
